content: The long-term implementation of certain interventions may present challenges. In specific contexts, the following references provide critical insights: 1. Baeten et al. conducted a systematic review of serodiscordant couples, focusing on the use of antiretroviral prophylaxis for HIV-1 prevention in heterosexual men and women. Their findings, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, highlight the efficacy of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in reducing HIV transmission risk. 2. The CDC website (2011) reported that both the CDC trial and another major study demonstrated that PrEP significantly reduces the risk of HIV infection among heterosexual individuals. This information was accessed on November 2, 2011. 3. The Family Health International (FHI) website (2011) announced the orderly closure of the FEM-PrEP trial, which was also accessed on November 2, 2011. 4. Grant et al. (2010) published findings in the New England Journal of Medicine on the effectiveness of pre-exposure chemoprophylaxis for HIV prevention among men who have sex with men (MSM). Their study demonstrated significant reductions in HIV acquisition. 5. The Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (2011) provides a methodological framework for evaluating interventions, including PrEP. 6. Baeten et al. (2011) characterized HIV-1 serodiscordant couples enrolled in a clinical trial of antiretroviral pre-exposure prophylaxis for HIV-1 prevention. Their findings, published in PLoS One, underscore the importance of targeted interventions in high-risk populations. 7. A 2007 study published in PLoS Clinical Trials evaluated the use of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for HIV prevention in women. This phase 2, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial demonstrated promising results. 8. The University of Washington website (2011) highlighted a pivotal study showing that HIV medications are highly effective as prophylaxis against HIV infection in men and women in Africa. This information was accessed on November 2, 2011. 9. Caitlin Kennedy and Virginia Tedrow (2012) conducted a systematic review to assess whether oral emtricitabine (FTC) and/or tenofovir (TDF) should be used in heterosexual serodiscordant couples. Their findings emphasize the high efficacy of these medications in reducing HIV transmission. 10. Baeten et al. (2012) reported a 67% reduction in HIV-1 acquisition with TDF and a 75% reduction with FTC/TDF compared to placebo in the Partners PrEP study. 11. Studies examining knowledge and attitudes toward PrEP among heterosexual individuals and serodiscordant couples are limited. However, qualitative interviews with 15 HIV-discordant heterosexual couples in Kenya revealed positive responses to PrEP, citing ease of administration as a major advantage. 12. A national telephone survey in the United States found that women with higher sexual risk behaviors expressed greater intent to use PrEP if available. Factors such as unprotected sex, multiple sexual partners, and involvement with high-risk male partners were associated with higher interest in PrEP. 13. Another survey among U.S. providers and consumers revealed that while less than 4% of consumers perceived themselves at high or medium risk for HIV, 42% expressed interest in using PrEP. Additionally, 88% of clinicians indicated willingness to prescribe PrEP to at-risk populations. 14. A study among truck drivers in India found that participants favored herpes simplex virus suppression over PrEP but were more willing to pay for PrEP than for circumcision. 15. Focus groups with at-risk African American youth in Atlanta revealed barriers to PrEP use, such as cost and dislike of oral medications. However, most participants expressed strong interest in daily antiretroviral use for HIV prevention if it were effective, accessible, and free. 16. Studies among MSM and transgender individuals in various countries, including the United States, Peru, Thailand, and Australia, have examined awareness and attitudes toward PrEP. Awareness of PrEP among MSM in the U.S. has increased over time, with 16%, 19%, and 36% reporting awareness in studies published in 2008, 2009, and 2011, respectively. 17. Early qualitative studies among MSM in the U.S. revealed polarized reactions to PrEP, with positive responses focusing on its user-friendliness and potential benefits in serodiscordant relationships, while negative reactions centered on concerns about side effects. 18. A study in Peru found that while PrEP was generally acceptable, concerns about sexual risk disinhibition, stigma, discrimination, and mistrust of healthcare professionals were significant barriers. Among those willing to use PrEP, over 35% reported they might decrease condom use while on PrEP. 19. Factors influencing PrEP acceptability include efficacy, potential side effects, and out-of-pocket costs. A study among iPrEx participants in the U.S. highlighted barriers such as stigma, co-occurring illnesses, and stress, while facilitators included establishing a routine and bundling PrEP with other medications. 20. Biomedical prevention methods, including PrEP, have shown promise in addressing the disproportionate burden of HIV among MSM and transgender women. PrEP, specifically, has proven effective in providing additional protection against HIV acquisition through unprotected rectal exposure. 21. Five clinical trials since 2005 have focused on the effectiveness of oral PrEP among injection drug users, serodiscordant couples, heterosexual women, and high-risk MSM. These trials have established the efficacy of oral emtricitabine (FTC) and tenofovir (TDF) in preventing HIV infection in high-risk populations.
